pos: n. (Bernardino Ochino, 1487–1564, vicar-general of the Capuchins who fled Rome for Geneva and ended his life in grave error)
etymology: Italian Bernardino, diminutive of Bernardo, bear-bold, from Germanic bern and hard; Ochino, a Sienese family name.
biblical_def: Bernardino Ochino was the most celebrated preacher in Italy before he was the most notorious. Three times vicar-general of the Capuchins, he preached Lent at Naples in 1536 and at Venice to crowds that emptied the other churches, and there he fell in with Juan de Valdés and Peter Martyr Vermigli and learned the free justification of the sinner. Summoned to Rome by the new Inquisition in 1542, he crossed the Alps instead, pastored the Italian congregation at Geneva, served Augsburg, and under Edward VI held a prebend at Canterbury. Mary's accession drove him back to Zurich, and there in 1563 he printed his Dialogi XXX, which handled the doctrine of the Trinity loosely and in one dialogue allowed that a man might in some case take a second wife. Zurich deprived him; he died of plague in Moravia among the Anabaptists. The dictionary honours the man who gave up a cardinal's prospects for the reproach of Christ and names the end without softening it: a flight from error is not yet an arrival at the truth, and a gifted preacher who will not be bound by a confessing church drifts. “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1Jo 2:19) is written of another case, but the warning stands over every unsettled man.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines apostasy as a total desertion of the faith one has professed, and heresy as a fundamental error in religion.
webster_full: APOS'TASY, n. An abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion or departure from one's faith or religion.
HER'ESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
PREACH'ER, n. One who discourses publicly on religious subjects; one who inculcates.
DRIFT, n. A driving; impulse; course of anything; tendency.
scriptures: They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us: but they went out, that they might be made manifest that they were not all of us.

But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction.
But we are not of them who draw back unto perdition; but of them that believe to the saving of the soul.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
corruption_summary: The great preacher who fled Rome and never arrived at a confession.
corruption_paragraphs: Ochino is regularly enlisted as an early hero of free inquiry, a man hounded by Geneva and Zurich as he had been by Rome, and the Dialogi are read as the first stirrings of liberty of conscience. The account will not stand. Zurich did not burn him and did not hunt him; a Reformed city removed a Reformed minister from a Reformed pulpit for printing what those churches confessed to be error about the Godhead and about marriage, which is discipline, not persecution. To call it persecution is to grant that a church owes its pulpit to any man who once suffered for the gospel.

The principle to recover is that courage does not sanctify doctrine. A man may be brave at Rome and wrong at Zurich, and the second does not cancel the first nor the first excuse the second. Paul fixes the measure where no reputation reaches it: “But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8).

pos: n. (Pietro Paolo Vergerio, c. 1498–1565, papal nuncio and bishop who became a Reformed publicist in Germany and the Slavic lands)
etymology: Italian Pietro, from Greek petros, a stone; Paolo, from Latin Paulus, little; Vergerio, an Istrian family name.
biblical_def: Pietro Paolo Vergerio met the Reformation first as its opponent. Sent as papal nuncio to Germany, he interviewed Luther at Wittenberg in 1535 and reported him with contempt; he was made bishop of Capodistria in his native Istria and laboured to recall his diocese to Rome. Reading the controversy in order to refute it undid him. By 1546 he was suspected, by 1549 deprived and excommunicated, and he fled to the Grisons and then to Switzerland. Duke Christoph of Württemberg took him as a counsellor, and from Tübingen he spent sixteen years writing against the papacy in the languages of the people and underwriting the Slovene and Croatian Scriptures that Primož Trubar and his fellows were preparing. He died at Tübingen in 1565. He is the type of a man whose office was his snare and whose study was his deliverance, and whose later usefulness lay not in a pulpit but in a press. The apostolic answer to the authority that had commissioned him was the answer he came to give: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a nuncio as an ambassador from the pope to an emperor or king, and a bishop as an overseer of a diocese.
webster_full: NUN'CIO, n. An ambassador from the pope to some prince or state; a messenger.
BISH'OP, n. An overseer; in the primitive church, a spiritual overseer; an elder or presbyter.
RECANT', v. To retract; to recall; to contradict a former declaration.
PRESS, n. An instrument or machine for printing; the art or business of printing.
scriptures: Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you,
Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt: for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward.
Rev 18:4
And I heard another voice from heaven, saying, Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues.
corruption_summary: The nuncio who read the Reformation to refute it and was converted by it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Where Vergerio is noticed at all he is handled as a careerist who changed sides when his preferment failed, which is a cheap reading of a man who exchanged a bishopric for exile and spent his remaining years on Slovene grammars and Croatian types that could profit him nothing.

The principle to recover is that a vernacular Bible is not a scholar's luxury but the ordinary means by which a people is called out, and that the call is a command before it is a comfort: “Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins” (Rev 18:4). Vergerio obeyed it late and at cost, and spent what was left of his life putting the summons into the hands of men who had never heard it in their own tongue.

pos: n. (Galeazzo Caracciolo, 1517–1586, Marquis of Vico, Neapolitan nobleman who left his estates and household for Geneva)
etymology: Italian Galeazzo, a Lombard given name; Caracciolo, one of the seven great houses of Naples.
biblical_def: Galeazzo Caracciolo, Marquis of Vico, was heir to one of the first houses of Naples and grandson of a pope's ally, with a place at the emperor's court and a wife and six children in his palace. Under the preaching of Peter Martyr Vermigli and in the circle of Juan de Valdés he was brought to the knowledge of the free justification of sinners, and for some years he tried what thousands tried: to hold the faith inwardly and the position outwardly. In 1551 he judged it impossible and went to Geneva, where he was received into the Italian congregation, made an elder, and became Calvin's intimate friend; Calvin dedicated to him the commentary on First Corinthians. His estates were confiscated, his father disinherited him, and his wife Vittoria would not follow or receive him when he travelled to plead with her. He lived thirty-five years a plain burgher in a small house and was buried without a monument. He is the clearest Italian instance of a man weighing the cost in advance and paying it: “whosoever he be of you that forsaketh not all that he hath, he cannot be my disciple” (Luk 14:33).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a marquis as a title of honour next below a duke, and to forsake as to quit or leave entirely.
webster_full: MAR'QUIS, n. A title of honour in Great Britain, France and other countries, next in rank below a duke.
FORSAKE', v. To quit or leave entirely; to desert; to abandon; to depart from.
EX'ILE, n. The person banished, or the state of being banished from one's country.
EL'DER, n. In the primitive church, one who had the oversight and care of a church.
scriptures: So likewise, whosoever he be of you that forsaketh not all that he hath, he cannot be my disciple.

And every one that hath forsaken houses, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name's sake, shall receive an hundredfold, and shall inherit everlasting life.
Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season;
Php 3:8

Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,
corruption_summary: The Marquis of Vico, who counted a Neapolitan palace loss for Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is nearer home: the Marquis is quoted in sermons as a proof that God rewards sacrifice, as though Geneva had paid him back in peace of mind for the palace he lost. It did not. He lost the estates and did not get the wife, and the record of his later years is of an elder doing unremarkable work in a crowded refugee congregation.

The principle to recover is that the hundredfold of Mat 19:29 is promised with persecutions and consummated in the life to come, not drawn as a dividend in this one. Paul says what the arithmetic actually is: “I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord” (Php 3:8). A man who expects an earthly balance will read his losses as evidence against God; a man who has counted them loss already is free.

pos: n. (Juan de Valdés, c. 1500–1541, Spanish humanist whose Naples circle carried the doctrine of free justification into Italy)
etymology: Spanish Juan, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Valdés, a house of Cuenca in Castile.
biblical_def: Juan de Valdés was a Castilian gentleman of Cuenca, twin or near-twin brother of the emperor's Latin secretary Alfonso. His Diálogo de doctrina cristiana of 1529 was condemned at Alcalá, and he left Spain in 1531 for Rome and then Naples, where from 1535 until his death in 1541 he gathered the most remarkable circle in Italy: Giulia Gonzaga, Ochino, Vermigli, Carnesecchi, Caracciolo. He taught the free pardon of the sinner on the ground of Christ's righteousness alone, and he taught it in a key of inward illumination, in conversation and in manuscripts passed hand to hand. He never separated from Rome, never reformed a service of worship, never gathered a church. When he died his disciples scattered three ways, and the three ways are the whole argument of this entry: some to Geneva and a confession, some to the stake, some back to the mass. Valdés saw the heart of the gospel and would not draw the consequence. “Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again” (Joh 3:7) he pressed, while leaving his hearers inside the house that denied it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines illumination as the act of enlightening the understanding, and justification as the act of absolving or clearing from guilt.
webster_full: ILLUMINA'TION, n. The act of illuminating; infusion of intellectual light; divine or supernatural enlightening.
JUSTIFICA'TION, n. In theology, remission of sin and absolution from guilt and punishment; acquittal.
CIR'CLE, n. A company; an assembly; as a circle of friends.
INWARD, a. Internal; interior; placed or being within; seated in the mind.
scriptures: Joh 3:7
Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again.
Rom 10:3
For they being ignorant of God's righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God.
Gal 2:16

Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away.
corruption_summary: The Naples master who taught free justification and never left the house that denied it.
corruption_paragraphs: Valdés is now claimed as the founder of a gentler, undogmatic, interior Christianity that the hard confessional parties of the sixteenth century betrayed on both sides — a spirituality without a church. The claim is answerable from the fate of his own circle. An inward gospel with no confession to state it, no discipline to guard it, and no congregation to shelter it left his disciples each to face the Inquisition alone, on his own resources, and most of them did not stand.

The principle to recover is that the gospel is a public thing with a public form, and that the form is not an accretion upon the life but the means of preserving it. Paul will not let the inward and the confessed be separated: “Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ” (Gal 2:16) is a doctrine to be said, and said in the hearing of men who deny it.

“going about to establish their own righteousness” (Rom 10:3) — the error he saw clearly.
“Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof” (2Ti 3:5) — the house he would not leave.

pos: n. (Celio Secondo Curione, 1503–1569, Piedmontese humanist, professor of rhetoric at Basel)
etymology: Italian from Latin Caelius, a Roman gens name; Secundus, second; Curione, from Latin curio, a herald.
biblical_def: Celio Secondo Curione was born at Cirie in Piedmont, the twenty-third child of a noble house, and came to the gospel through a Bible and a copy of Luther that he found as a student at Turin. He was twice imprisoned and twice got free, once by substituting a bundle of bones for a venerated relic and once by walking out of a cell in his keeper's clothes, and the stories were told against him afterwards by men who preferred their martyrs quieter. He taught at Pavia and Lucca, fled Italy in 1542 in the same alarm that scattered Ochino and Vermigli, and from 1547 held the chair of rhetoric at Basel until his death. There he trained a generation in Latin letters, edited the writings of the young Olympia Morata, and published against the Inquisition. He stood close to the Italian circles at Basel that were sliding toward anti-Trinitarian opinions and did not slide: he stayed in the communion of the Basel church and died in it. He is the dictionary's instance of learning held in its place: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rhetoric as the art of speaking with propriety and elegance, and a humanist as one versed in the knowledge of human nature and letters.
webster_full: RHET'ORIC, n. The art of speaking with propriety, elegance and force; the power of persuasion.
LET'TERS, n. Learning; erudition; as a man of letters.
PROFESS'OR, n. One that publicly teaches any science or branch of learning in a college.
WIS'DOM, n. The right use or exercise of knowledge; in theology, the knowledge of God.
scriptures: Pro 9:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?
corruption_summary: The Piedmontese rhetorician who kept his learning under the fear of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Curione is handled in the literature chiefly as a conduit between Italian humanism and the heterodox Italian colony at Basel, which quietly converts a man's acquaintances into his opinions. He is better read the other way: a scholar whose friends went where he declined to follow.

The principle to recover is that learning is a servant with a master, and that the fear of the LORD is not a pious preface to study but the thing that orders it. Paul puts the warning where a professor of rhetoric would feel it: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men” (Col 2:8). The remedy is not less study but study under a word that judges it.

“Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” (Col 2:8) — the warning in a rhetorician's chair.
“rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15) — the labour that outlasts eloquence.

pos: n. (Francesco Spiera, d. 1548, lawyer of Cittadella who recanted the gospel before the Inquisition and died in despair)
etymology: Italian Francesco, the Frenchman, from Late Latin Franciscus; Spiera, a Venetian family name.
biblical_def: Francesco Spiera was a prosperous lawyer of Cittadella in the Venetian territory, a man of standing with a large family, who received the doctrine of free justification and did not keep it to himself but taught it to his neighbours for some years. Delated to the Inquisition, he was examined at Venice in 1548, and under the threat of ruin he abjured, read his recantation publicly in his own town, and went home. From that hour he fell into a horror that no argument reached. He said he had sinned against the Holy Ghost, that Christ was not for him, that he was already a reprobate; he refused food, grew emaciated, and died before the year was out. Vergerio attended him and published the case; Calvin and Curione both wrote upon it; it was printed in English within a generation and preached from for two centuries. The dictionary records it as the sixteenth century did, as the plainest commentary in that age on a single sentence: “But whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:33).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines despair as a hopelessness, a desperation, and to recant as to retract a former declaration.
webster_full: DESPAIR', n. Hopelessness; a hopeless state; a destitution of hope or expectation.
RECANTA'TION, n. A retraction of a former declaration; a declaration that contradicts a former one.
ABJURE', v. To renounce upon oath; to abandon; to retract or recant.
RE'PROBATE, n. One not predestinated to salvation; a wicked abandoned person.
scriptures: But whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven.
For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.
The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity; but a wounded spirit who can bear?
Heb 6:6
If they shall fall away, to renew them again unto repentance; seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame.
corruption_summary: The recanting lawyer whose despair the Reformers preached as a warning.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern handling of Spiera turns him into a casualty of Protestant severity: a frightened man driven mad, it is said, by a doctrine of election that left him no door, and the Reformers who published his case are charged with using a sick man to frighten others. The charge mistakes who frightened him. It was not Geneva that put him to the choice between his estate and his confession, and it was not a doctrine of election that he broke under but an oath he swore against what he knew to be true.

The principle to recover is the distinction Paul draws between two sorrows, which is precisely the diagnostic Spiera could not apply to himself: “For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death” (2Co 7:10). Despair is not a deeper repentance; it is the counterfeit, and it ends where Spiera ended. The remedy preached to such a man is not a lighter view of his sin but a larger view of the blood that answers it.

pos: n. (Pietro Carnesecchi, 1508–1567, Florentine protonotary and Valdésian, beheaded and burned at Rome)
etymology: Italian Pietro, from Greek petros, a stone; Carnesecchi, a Florentine house, from carne secca, dried flesh.
biblical_def: Pietro Carnesecchi rose young and high: protonotary apostolic and first secretary to Clement VII, with benefices in France and the friendship of queens. At Naples he joined the circle of Juan de Valdés and never afterwards believed what Rome required him to profess. He was tried for heresy in 1546 and acquitted through the favour of Paul III, tried again under Julius III and again acquitted, and lived for twenty years in Venice, Paris and Florence as a marked man who was never quite taken. In 1566 Cosimo I de' Medici, wanting the new pope's goodwill and a grand-ducal crown, arrested his own guest at table and sent him to Rome. Pius V had the trial completed; Carnesecchi, offered his life for a recantation, refused it, and on 1 October 1567 was beheaded in the Piazza di Ponte and his body burned. He is the Valdésian who at last did what his master never required of him. “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a martyr as one who suffers death in defence of the Christian faith, and testimony as a solemn declaration to establish a fact.
webster_full: MAR'TYR, n. One who suffers death in defence of the Christian faith, or in defence of any cause.
TES'TIMONY, n. A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact.
PROTH'ONOTARY, n. The chief notary; in the Roman chancery, one of twelve officers who register pontifical acts.
CONFESS', v. To own, acknowledge or avow, as a crime, a fault, a charge, or the truth of a doctrine.
scriptures: Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven.
And ye shall be brought before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony against them and the Gentiles.
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.

But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.
corruption_summary: The pope's own secretary who died rather than unsay the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The nearer misuse is the sentimental one: Carnesecchi is told as a story about Medici treachery, a guest betrayed at his host's table, with the doctrine he died for left out as a detail of the period. Betrayal was the occasion; the cause was that he would not say the mass saved him.

The principle to recover is that confession is the act by which faith becomes public and costly, and that the promise attached to it is not deliverance but acknowledgment before the Father. The Lord sets the two sides of it side by side in one breath, and Carnesecchi, who had twenty years to think about it, took the side that cost him his head: “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:32).

“And ye shall be brought before governors and kings for my sake” (Mat 10:18) — three tribunals in twenty years.

pos: n. (Aonio Paleario, c. 1503–1570, humanist and schoolmaster, hanged and burned at Rome)
etymology: A grecised pen-name: Greek Aonios, of Aonia, the Muses' country, for Antonio; Paleario for della Paglia, of the straw.
biblical_def: Aonio Paleario was born Antonio della Paglia at Veroli and took a scholar's Greek name, as the humanists did. He taught the classics at Siena, Lucca and Milan for forty years, wrote a celebrated Latin poem on the immortality of the soul, and was repeatedly delated for heresy by colleagues who resented him and clergy who had read him. At Siena in 1542, answering the first charge, he said that the cause he was accused of was the cause of Christ and that his only plea was the cross; the sentence is the reason he is remembered. He survived that trial and the next, but in 1567 he was taken to Rome, held three years, and in 1570 hanged and his body burned. He wrote no system and founded no church; he was a grammar-master who would not teach a boy that the mass took away sin. “But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal 6:14) is the text his life was an argument for.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the cross as the ensign of the Christian religion and the atonement of Christ, and a schoolmaster as one who presides over a school.
webster_full: CROSS, n. The ensign of the Christian religion; hence, figuratively, the religion itself; the sufferings of Christ.
SCHOOLMASTER, n. The man who presides over and teaches a school; a teacher, instructor, preceptor.
GLO'RY, v. To boast; to exult with joy; to rejoice; to be proud of.
RE'PROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt or derision; shame; infamy; disgrace.
scriptures: Gal 6:14
But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world.
For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach.
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
corruption_summary: The schoolmaster whose only plea at the bar was the cross of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Paleario is usually filed among the Italian humanists, with his death treated as the price of free thought rather than the price of a doctrine, so that the Latin poet survives in the histories and the confessor does not.

The principle to recover is that a man's learning is not his plea and his reputation is not his covering. Paleario had both in abundance and set them aside for the only ground that holds in a court or at a stake: “For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1Co 2:2). The writer to the Hebrews names the direction such a resolution always takes a man — “Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb 13:13).

pos: n. (Giovanni Mollio of Montalcino, c. 1500–1553, Franciscan professor burned at Rome for preaching justification by faith)
etymology: Italian Giovanni, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Mollio, latinised from Molli, of Montalcino in Tuscany.
biblical_def: Giovanni Mollio of Montalcino entered the Franciscans young and became one of the order's best lecturers, reading divinity at Brescia, Milan and Bologna. Expounding the epistle to the Romans in the university at Bologna he taught the justification of the sinner by faith without the deeds of the law, and the students carried it through the city. He was silenced, examined, and in 1543 recanted under pressure — a fact the dictionary does not omit, because what follows is the point. He went back to preaching the same doctrine, was arrested again, and in September 1553 stood before the tribunal of eight cardinals at Rome. Offered his life once more, he answered them in a speech that the reports preserve, charging them with selling for money what Christ gave freely; the sentence was passed, and he was burned in the Campo de' Fiori with a Perugian weaver named Tisserano. A man who had once drawn back stood the second time. “For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth” (Rom 1:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the gospel as the history of the birth, life, actions, death and resurrection of Christ, and faith as the assent of the mind to the truth of divine revelation.
webster_full: GOS'PEL, n. The history of the birth, life, actions, death, resurrection and ascension of Jesus Christ; the good news of salvation.
FAITH, n. The assent of the mind to the truth of what God has revealed; evangelical, justifying or saving faith.
FRI'AR, n. An appellation common to the monks of all the religious orders; a brother.
STAKE, n. A post; the post to which one condemned to be burnt is bound.
scriptures: Rom 1:16
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Act 4:20
For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.
Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
corruption_summary: The Franciscan of Bologna who recanted once and stood the second time.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation in telling Mollio's story is the opposite one: to leave the recantation out, so that the martyr arrives on the page already finished. The sources do not allow it, and the gospel does not need it.

The principle to recover is that a fall is not the end of a man whom God has begun with, and that restoration is ordinarily to the very post he abandoned. Mollio was not given some quieter service after Bologna; he was sent back to the same lecture and the same text, and the second time he did not move. “Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28) was the sentence he had unsaid, and it was the sentence he died saying.

“For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:20) — why the silencing failed.

pos: n. (Pomponio Algerio, c. 1531–1556, law student of Padua, executed at Rome in boiling oil)
etymology: Italian from Latin Pomponius, a Roman gens name; Algerio, a family of Nola in Campania.
biblical_def: Pomponio Algerio was a student of civil law at Padua, from Nola in the kingdom of Naples, twenty-four years old and not a minister or a scholar of any note. He had received the gospel and spoke of it among the students; he was denounced, arrested by the Venetian authorities in 1555, and when Rome demanded him the Republic gave him up. He was repeatedly offered his life for a recantation by men who had no wish to kill a boy, and he repeatedly declined, and one of the letters he wrote from the prison at Venice survives, in which he says that his dungeon is a pleasant garden and his chains an ornament. On 22 August 1556 he was put to death in the Piazza Navona by being lowered into a cauldron of boiling oil, pitch and turpentine. The dictionary records him because he is the test case against every account of the Reformation as a quarrel of professors: the thing that was at stake was plain enough for a law student to die for. “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Act 7:59) is the only commentary he needed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cauldron as a large kettle or boiler, and constancy as a firmness of mind, fixedness in purpose or affection.
webster_full: CAL'DRON, n. A large kettle or boiler, of copper or other metal.
CON'STANCY, n. Fixedness; a standing firm; firmness of mind; stability in attachment or purpose.
STU'DENT, n. A person engaged in study; one who is devoted to learning.
AFFLIC'TION, n. The cause of continued pain of body or mind; calamity; the state of being afflicted.
scriptures: Act 7:59
And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.
Rom 8:18
For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.
But rejoice, inasmuch as ye are partakers of Christ's sufferings; that, when his glory shall be revealed, ye may be glad also with exceeding joy.
Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place.
corruption_summary: The Padua law student who called his dungeon a garden.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Where Algerio appears in modern accounts his age and his manner of death do the work, and the content of what he refused to unsay is passed over — which turns a confessor into a curiosity of penal history.

The principle to recover is the apostolic arithmetic of suffering, which is not a stoic contempt for pain but a comparison in which pain is outweighed: “For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom 8:18). That is the ground on which a prison is called a garden. The psalm says the same from the other side of it: “we went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place” (Psa 66:12).

“the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom 8:18) — the reckoning in his prison letter.
“we went through fire and through water” (Psa 66:12) — the psalm the Italian churches sang over their dead.
